content.thinking:
I'm checking what users actually saw: requests took longer, especially on the shop pages, while failure rates stayed flat. I'm now trying to phrase the symptom without naming the cause, so something like "shop requests grew slow" should do it.

I'm now laying out the causal chain: requests to the shop service slowed as its memory climbed toward the container limit, with no rise in failures. I'm checking whether any deploy or flag change lines up with the onset, and whether a restart relieving the pressure fits in-process memory growth.

I'm working out the causal chain now: memory in the shop service grew steadily with no matching rise in traffic, and I'm checking whether anything changed that could explain it. The deploy and flag records show nothing new in the window, so there's no change to point at. I'm now looking at a module-level cache that keeps growing with each account page render, which would explain why only a restart clears the pressure. That mechanism still rests on a reading I haven't actually verified, so I'm treating it as a candidate rather than a confirmed root cause.

I'm tracing the mechanism now: the account page path calls record_visit on every render, success or failure, and that adds each new shopper to a module-level dict that only a restart clears, so memory keeps growing. The reading behind this is still unrun, so I'm holding it as the likely cause rather than a confirmed one.

I'm now writing up the contributing factors, starting with how the memory growth was caught: an alert that waits for the condition to hold before firing, with nobody paged.

I'm weighing whether the alert setup belongs among the contributing factors: no latency alert was seen firing, so the slowdown was caught only through the memory alert.

I'm weighing whether the slowdown should count as its own contributing factor: no latency alert was seen firing, so the memory alert was the only thing that caught it, and only after its 15-minute hold. I'm also noting that nothing in the record shows a test that would catch unbounded growth in the in-process store before the change went out.

I'm settling on the memory-growth check as a missing safeguard: nothing in the record shows a soak test watching memory across many distinct shoppers before release, so I'm proposing one that fails if resident memory keeps climbing. I'm leaving the missing paging out of the contributing factors, since a page would not have shortened the response, and listing it under what went wrong with an action item instead.

I'm drafting the action items now: an alert on the shop's request latency against its baseline, a memory-growth trend alert for the same service, a soak test that fails if memory keeps climbing across many shoppers, and routing the high-memory alert to on-call paging.

I'm drafting the lessons now, starting with what went well: the restart was confirmed as the mitigation that worked, and Argus checked the flag provider's history to rule out flag changes. I'm also noting that nobody was paged, and that the investigation never pinned down the specific allocation behind the growth.

I'm weighing whether the memory-growth finding, the latency slowdown, and the missing paging each belong in the record as their own items. I'm checking which of these points are actually supported and which are only inferred from timing.

I'm checking the remaining assumptions: the link from memory growth to the latency slowdown rests on timing and the alert record, not on a shown mechanism, and the traffic-flatness point comes from the investigator's read rather than a measurement. I'm also noting that the log window only covers the early part of the incident.

I'm settling the causal chain as three steps: shoppers' requests took longer, most of all on the shop pages, while the io-shop process's resident memory climbed steadily toward its container limit. I'm also noting that no deploy or flag change lines up with the onset, and that the growth sat inside the running process, since restarting io-shop cleared it.

I'm writing up the causal chain's last step: the memory growth came from the account page path, where each render adds the shopper to a module-level store that only a restart clears. I'm keeping this as the likely mechanism rather than a confirmed one, since the reading behind it hasn't been run.

I'm settling the last step as the root-cause mechanism: the account page path calls record_visit on every render, and by the code-fix reading that adds the shopper to a module-level store that only a restart empties. I'm keeping it flagged as a reading, since the record doesn't show the allocation directly.

action_items.item: Add an alert on io-shop request latency at the slow percentiles, compared with its normal level.
Add an alert that fires when io-shop's resident memory is on course to reach its container limit, based on its growth trend.
Add a soak test to the release pipeline that renders account pages for a large number of different shoppers and fails if the process's resident memory keeps growing.
Route HighMemoryUsage on io-shop to the on-call paging rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' requests to io-shop took longer from the onset, and the slowest requests slowed down the most.
Requests slowed while the io-shop process's resident memory climbed steadily toward its container limit.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release of io-shop: none came back for the day before the onset.
A feature flag change: the flag provider showed no flag changes by anyone but Argus in the hour leading up to the investigation, an hour that includes the onset.

causal_chain.step: The memory built up inside the running process, not because of a change to production: no deploy or flag change was found, and restarting io-shop brought the service back down from the incident's level.

Memory grew with every new shopper served an account page: serve_account_page calls record_visit on every render, on failure and on success, and according to Code-Fix's reading record_visit adds the shopper to a module-level store that only a restart empties.

input.cause_in_plain_words: The shop's memory kept filling up until the shop slowed down, most likely because it kept a note of every shopper who opened their account page and only cleared those notes when it was restarted.

contributing_factors.factor: The slowdown was found only by the memory alert, which waits for its condition to hold before it fires. No alert on io-shop request latency, or on how fast memory was growing toward the limit, was seen firing.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: An alert on request latency or on the memory trend would have flagged the slowdown sooner, so the restart could have come earlier and the incident would have been shorter.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that runs io-shop against many different shoppers for a long time and watches whether its memory keeps growing before code is released.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A store that grows without limit on the account page path would have been caught before it reached production.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: The Mitigation Agent restarted io-shop to act on C1, the leading candidate.
The Mitigation Agent checked the service afterwards, found it no longer at the incident's level, and judged the restart CONFIRMED.
Argus read the flag provider's history, which showed that no flag change by anyone else came before the incident.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #542.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was brought in.

input.root_cause: serve_account_page calls record_visit on every account page render, on failure and on success (U1, U2), and according to Code-Fix's reading record_visit adds each new shopper to `_LAST_SEEN`, a module-level dict in `src/io_shop/visits.py` that nothing but `forget_every_visit()` empties. That means the process's resident memory keeps growing with every new shopper until a restart, and requests slow down as it nears the container limit.
input.still_at_risk: Until a fix is in place, the shop's memory can climb toward its limit again after the restart and slow requests the same way.
input.symptom: Shop requests slowed down for shoppers
